title: Factory Method Pattern
oneLiner: Lets a class defer object construction to subclasses, so calling code never has to know a concrete type to create it.

hero.name: Forge Master
hero.catchphrase: Why are you constructing everything yourself? Give me the blueprint. I'll handle creation.
hero.power: Summons the right object for the job from a blueprint, without the caller ever naming the concrete class.
hero.weakness: Every new product type needs a new creator subclass — Forge Master can multiply the class count if wielded carelessly.
hero.origin: Born in a payment service riddled with 'if (provider === "stripe")' branches, Forge Master appeared to hand construction over to specialists instead.

story.problem: PaymentService constructs a `new StripeGateway()` directly. Adding Razorpay means editing PaymentService's internals again, and again for every provider after that.
story.solution: Forge Master gives each payment provider its own creator. PaymentService just asks for 'a gateway' — it never touches 'new StripeGateway()' again.
story.result: Adding a new payment provider means adding a new creator class. The core service never changes.

before: PaymentService edited for every new provider
Tight coupling to every concrete gateway class
Risk of regressions in unrelated providers
after: New providers ship as new files, zero edits to PaymentService
PaymentService depends only on the PaymentGateway interface
Existing providers stay untouched and untested-safe

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: PaymentService is riddled with construction logic for every provider it knows about.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Every time we add a payment provider, I have to reopen PaymentService and add another if-branch. This file is 400 lines of constructors now.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Forge Master steps out of the blueprint vault, hammer raised.
panels.speaker: Forge Master
panels.dialogue: Stop building gateways with your bare hands. Define the blueprint — I'll forge the right one at the right time.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: An abstract createGateway() method appears. Each provider gets its own creator subclass that overrides it.
panels.speaker: Forge Master
panels.dialogue: PaymentService only calls createGateway(). It has no idea — and no need to know — which concrete class comes back.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Razorpay support ships as a brand-new file. PaymentService.ts isn't touched at all.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We added Razorpay without editing a single line of the existing payment code. New file, zero regressions.

useWhen: A class can't anticipate which concrete type of object it needs to create ahead of time.
You want to let subclasses (or plugins) specify the objects they create, without touching shared code.
Construction logic is complex enough that it deserves its own dedicated method or class.
avoidWhen: There's only ever going to be one concrete product — a plain constructor call is simpler and clearer.
The extra creator-class hierarchy adds more ceremony than the variation in construction actually warrants.
A simple factory function or a lookup object (map of type -> constructor) already solves the problem without subclassing.
commonMistakes: Reaching for full Factory Method (with abstract creator subclasses) when a simple factory function would do — not every 'thing that creates objects' needs the formal pattern.
Letting the factory method leak concrete implementation details back up to the caller, defeating the whole point.
Creating a new creator subclass per product without ever consolidating shared construction logic in the base class.
Confusing Factory Method (subclasses override one creation method) with Abstract Factory (a family of related creation methods).
explanation.realWorldExample: Document editors that support multiple file formats (e.g. `createDocument()` overridden per format), UI toolkits that create platform-specific buttons, and ORMs that create the right query builder per database driver, all lean on Factory Method.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So Forge Master doesn't create the object himself?

conversation.speaker: Forge Master
conversation.message: Correct. I define the blueprint — the createGateway() method — and let each specialist creator fill it in for their own provider.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't that just a fancy if-statement in disguise?

conversation.speaker: Forge Master
conversation.message: The difference is where the branching lives. With an if-statement, PaymentService has to know every provider. With me, PaymentService knows none of them — it just asks, and trusts the creator it was given.

codeBattle.scenario: Your image-processing app needs to instantiate a different Exporter class depending on output format (PNG, JPEG, WebP), and new formats keep getting requested by the product team.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Forge Master lets you add a new Exporter subclass per format without ever touching the code that decides which exporter to construct.

quiz.question: What problem does Factory Method primarily solve?
options: Code that has to construct different concrete classes gets tightly coupled to every one of them
Two objects need to stay in sync with each other automatically
An object needs to change its behavior at runtime
A complex subsystem needs a simpler interface
quiz.answer: Code that has to construct different concrete classes gets tightly coupled to every one of them
quiz.explanation: Factory Method removes that coupling by pushing the 'which concrete class' decision into a dedicated creation method.

quiz.question: In Factory Method, who decides which concrete product gets created?
options: A subclass (or override) of the creator, via the factory method
The calling code, by passing a class reference directly
A global configuration file read at startup
The product classes themselves, via static methods
quiz.answer: A subclass (or override) of the creator, via the factory method
quiz.explanation: The creator defines the factory method as abstract (or with a default); subclasses override it to return the specific product.

quiz.question: You only ever need to construct one kind of Logger, with no variation now or planned. What's the better call?
options: Skip Factory Method — a plain constructor is simpler and equally correct
Always use Factory Method for every class that gets instantiated
Use Factory Method plus Singleton together no matter what
Refactor Logger into an interface with ten creator subclasses just in case
quiz.answer: Skip Factory Method — a plain constructor is simpler and equally correct
quiz.explanation: Factory Method earns its complexity when construction actually varies. With no variation, a direct constructor is clearer.

quiz.question: What's a common mistake when applying Factory Method?
options: Reaching for the full pattern (creator subclass hierarchy) when a simple factory function would solve the same problem
Using 'new' inside the factory method itself
Returning an interface type from the factory method
quiz.answer: Reaching for the full pattern (creator subclass hierarchy) when a simple factory function would solve the same problem
quiz.explanation: Not every creation problem needs formal subclassing — over-applying the pattern adds unnecessary class hierarchy.
